_title: Ten layouts that leave the dots behind (16 November)
_intro: The other 70 layouts place the number n and colour it prime or not. Such a picture can only show where primes are dense: lines, remainder classes, polynomials. These ten show what it cannot: the order of consecutive primes (words of gaps and of remainders), two primes at once (reversals, Goldbach pairs), how evenly the primes fill long windows, and the zeros. Each note on the page computes its numbers live; every number below was recomputed by a separate Python script.
_reveal: Does this reveal anything? No new mystery, and nothing about the Mersenne exponents: where they could be tested they behave like other primes (13 of the 52 have a prime reversal in base 10 where 14.1 are expected, 16 in base 2 where 20.4 are). What the ten pictures do show is where the open part of the primes sits. Seven are pure sieve: a rule of remainders, plus coin flips for whatever the rule allows, reproduces them in full (the dust of the gaps, the remainder words, the gap pairs, the opening that recurs, Goldbach's first partner, the reversals, the survivors). Two are not: the rows of the scales narrow in a way that no sieve with coin flips above it copies, and the spectrum shows the cause, the zeros. The atlas sits between: its columns are the sieve, but their counts scatter less than coin flips. So the border runs here: all local structure is the sieve; what remains is how evenly the primes fill long windows, and that is the zeros. Along the way three statements were derived first and tested after, and two numbers were measured; they are in the card below the table.
found: Classes push each other away, by their conductors
heuristic; derived first, tested after; literature not searched

Count the primes of class a mod q, each with weight ln p, in a window of H numbers near x. Split into characters, with independent zeros for different L-functions and the variance H·(ln(q<sub>χ</sub>·x/H) + 1 − γ − ln 2π) of Montgomery and Soundararajan for a character of conductor q<sub>χ</sub>, the covariance of two classes is Cov(a, b) = (H/φ(q)²)·T(b/a) for a ≠ b, with T(r) = Σ χ(r)·ln q<sub>χ</sub> over the characters χ ≠ χ₀ mod q. It depends neither on H nor on x. Mod 12: T(5) = ln 4 − ln 3 − ln 12 = −2.20, T(7) = −2 ln 4 = −2.77, T(11) = 0: the classes a and −a, the two halves of a lane of the cosine rows, are uncorrelated. Mod 8: −1.39, −2.77, −1.39 for r = 3, 5, 7. Mod 5: −1.61 for every pair.
The rule 'sieve, then a coin' carries over to Goldbach

The rule that gives the prime gaps (the next prime is the first survivor of the sieve that a coin accepts) is applied to the search for the smallest prime p with n − p prime: try p fails for certain if n − p has a prime factor up to 47, and otherwise succeeds with chance 1/(ln(n − p)·∏(1 − 1/q)), the product over the primes q up to 47.

For 4,000 random even n between 100,000 and 500,000 the chance of needing more than 1, 5, 10, 20 and 40 tries is 0.840, 0.387, 0.160, 0.033 and 0.0018 predicted, and 0.839, 0.385, 0.157, 0.033 and 0.0018 found; mean 6.09 tries against 6.09.
A short period ties a number to its reversal

The textbook factor for 'the reversal of a prime is prime' uses the primes that divide B² − 1 (3 and 11 in base 10, 3 in base 2). While the digits are few, every prime q with a short period in base B (B<sup>k</sup> ≡ 1 mod q for a small k) ties n to its reversal as well, because the few digit sums it depends on are far from evenly spread mod q.

Among the 20-bit primes the reversal is a multiple of 7 for 11.0% (an even share is 14.3%), of 5 for 17.9% (20.0%), of 31 for 2.5% (3.2%); in base 10 with 7 digits a multiple of 101 for 0.65% (0.99%). Reversible primes with 15 / 18 / 20 bits: 589 / 2,814 / 9,210; the textbook factor gives 479 / 2,651 / 8,552, and with the measured shares for 5, 7, 17, 31, 73, 127, 11 and 13 it gives 568 / 2,874 / 9,175.
Counts along a polynomial scatter far less than chance

In the atlas, the prime counts of the 1,250 polynomials differ from the Bateman–Horn prediction by 0.39 standard deviations of a random count, not 1 (the polygon spirals gave 0.6). Small primes hit a polynomial in a fixed rhythm; they do not draw lots.
The waves in the long rows of the scales are the zeta zeros

The bottom rows rebuilt from the first 160 zeta zeros alone, with no prime: correlation 0.940 (H = 16,384), 0.904 (8,192), 0.841 (4,096, where zeros up to height 770 would be needed and 334 were used).

cards.name: Chaos game of the gaps (mod 6)
cards.short: Gaps ≡ 2 and ≡ 4 (mod 6) take turns: a dust of dimension 1 where random gaps draw Sierpinski's triangle
cards.seen: Two thin legs made of short strokes, and every stroke is again two rows of strokes (right: the top, six times enlarged). The middle is empty. Gaps drawn at random would fill Sierpinski's triangle.
cards.explained: A point jumps half-way to one of three corners, chosen by the gap from the prime before: the top for a gap ≡ 0 (mod 6), bottom left for ≡ 2, bottom right for ≡ 4. Every prime from 5 on is ≡ 1 or 5 (mod 6); a gap ≡ 2 leads from 5 to 1 and a gap ≡ 4 from 1 to 5, so the two take turns, with any number of gaps ≡ 0 between them. A word of k gap classes is then a choice, at each step, between 0 and the one step allowed: 2·2<sup>k</sup> − 1 words, not 3<sup>k</sup>, and the picture has dimension 1, not 1.585.
cards.checked: Up to 500,000: 0 exceptions; of the 6,561 words of 8 classes exactly 511 occur, all that the rule allows. The classes 0, 2, 4 are used 17,087, 12,224 and 12,224 times. As a chain: after a gap ≡ 0 the next is ≡ 0, 2, 4 in 6,496, 5,315 and 5,275 cases; after ≡ 2 it is ≡ 0 in 5,275 and ≡ 4 in 6,949; after ≡ 4, 5,316 and 6,908. The allowed step is taken 57% of the time, a 0 only 43%: the ink along the strokes is uneven, and that part is Hardy–Littlewood.

cards.name: Chaos game of the remainders (mod P)
cards.short: Words of consecutive remainders: repeats 14.3% instead of 25%, at every scale
cards.seen: A cloud with a faint chequer: a thin patch in the outer corner of each quarter, and the same again inside every smaller square (right: the top-left corner, four times enlarged; one million numbers).
cards.explained: Four corners for the remainders 1, 5, 7, 11 (mod 12). The quarter a prime lands in is its own remainder, the quarter inside it the remainder of the prime before, and so on, so each word of remainders has its own square. A repeat needs a gap that is a multiple of 12, so the squares that point at their own corner are thin. Every step has a cheapest gap: 5 → 7 and 11 → 1 are the twin primes, 1 → 5 and 7 → 11 the gap 4, and the steps by 6 come third because a prime may stand in between.
cards.checked: Up to 500,000: repeats 14.3%. Steps as multiples of an even share, rows from 1, 5, 7, 11: 0.56 1.32 1.07 1.02 / 0.89 0.58 1.46 1.07 / 1.07 1.02 0.58 1.34 / 1.46 1.08 0.89 0.57. Of the steps 5 → 7, 59% are twin gaps; of 1 → 5, 66% are gaps of 4; of 1 → 7, 67% gaps of 6; of 1 → 1, 72% gaps of 12. A run of primes and its mirror image are equally common: 1 → 5 against 7 → 11 gives 3,428 and 3,486, 1 → 1 against 11 → 11 gives 1,464 and 1,478.

cards.name: Gap before against gap after
cards.short: A chequerboard: two cells in nine are empty, equal neighbours 0.43 times as common as chance
cards.seen: A chequerboard of squares, largest at the lower left and along the lines of 6, 12, 18, …; two cells in nine are empty and the diagonal is thin (right: the lower left, three times enlarged).
cards.explained: Each prime sits in the cell of its two gaps, the one before it across and the one after it upwards; a square's area is the number of primes with that pair. After a gap ≡ 2 (mod 6) the prime is ≡ 1, so the next gap is not ≡ 2; after ≡ 4 it is not ≡ 4. Equal gaps are three primes in arithmetic progression, which needs a multiple of 6. The picture is the same on both sides of the diagonal, because a run of primes and its mirror image are equally likely.
cards.checked: Up to 500,000 (41,534 primes from 7 on): the empty cells hold 0 primes. By class of the two gaps (0, 2, 4 mod 6; rows: the gap before): 6,496 5,315 5,275 / 5,275 0 6,949 / 5,316 6,908 0. Fullest cells: (6, 6) 1,115, (4, 6) 1,026, (6, 4) 1,017, (4, 2) 883, (2, 10) 864, (10, 2) 855, (2, 4) 827. Mirror symmetry over the 138 pairs of cells with 20 primes or more: χ² = 113 on 138. Equal gaps: 1,668, every one a multiple of 6, against 3,841 for the same gaps in random order.

cards.name: The opening recurs
cards.short: Primes whose next gaps copy 2, 4, 2, 4, 6, 2, …: nested constellations, at most 15 primes long
cards.verdict: Hardy–Littlewood; the limit of 15 is a theorem
cards.seen: A dense top row, then rows thinning fast; one dot alone on the bottom row (right: around it, four times enlarged).
cards.explained: Row L holds the primes whose next L gaps are the first gaps after 11: 2, 4, 2, 4, 6, 2, …. So row 1 and below are the twin primes, row 2 and below the triplets (p, p + 2, p + 6), row 3 and below the quadruplets, and so on: prime constellations, nested. The opening can come back because the first primes are the survivors of a wheel and a wheel repeats. It cannot come back once the stretch takes every remainder of some small prime: from 11 that happens with the 16th prime, so at most 15 primes (11 to 67) recur.
cards.checked: Recounted in Python: rows 36,971 / 3,738 / 723 / 80 / 18 / 2 / 1, as on the page. Nested counts against Hardy–Littlewood: 2 primes 4,562 (4,622 predicted), 3: 825 (856), 4: 101 (109), 5: 21 (24.5), 6: 3 (4.2), 7: 1 (1.6). The one stretch of 7 starts at 165,701. The 9 primes 11 to 41 come back at 182,403,491; the 15 are expected near 10^20.

cards.name: Goldbach's first partner
cards.short: Even n by the smallest prime p with n − p prime: empty rows by remainder, coin flips for the rest
cards.verdict: theorem (the empty places); the rule 'sieve, then a coin' (nothing fitted)
cards.seen: Rows thinning downwards like rain. Enlarged 14 times (right; light = multiple of 6): the top row is all dark, the rows below mix light and dark.
cards.explained: Row p is empty wherever a small prime divides n − p for certain: at the multiples of p, and, when 3 does not divide n, in every row p ≡ n (mod 3). So row 3 holds no multiple of 6; a number ≡ 1 (mod 3) never sits in the rows 7, 13, 19, 31, … and a number ≡ 2 (mod 3) never in the rows 5, 11, 17, 23, …. Among the tries that the small primes allow, each succeeds like the flip of a coin.
cards.checked: Recounted: multiples of 3 need 4.79 tries on average and the others 6.35; 24.9% of the others succeed at once, with 3; no n ≡ 1 (mod 3) has a partner ≡ 1 and no n ≡ 2 a partner ≡ 2 (0 exceptions). The worst case is 413,572 = 389 + 413,183, the 76th try (OEIS A025018). With the rule of the gaps and nothing fitted (fail for certain if n − p has a factor up to 47, otherwise succeed with chance 1/(ln(n − p)·∏(1 − 1/q))), the chance of more than 1, 5, 10, 20, 40 tries is 0.840, 0.387, 0.160, 0.033, 0.0018 predicted and 0.839, 0.385, 0.157, 0.033, 0.0018 found.

cards.name: Mirror: n against its digits reversed
cards.short: Four bands, four blocks; a reversal is 4.13 times as likely to be prime (base 10), and short periods tie the two further
cards.verdict: theorem (bands, 3 and 11); the count is heuristic
cards.seen: Base 10 (left, to 100,000): the primes lie in four bands, at the heights 0.1, 0.3, 0.7 and 0.9, and the green dots (the reversal is prime too) stand in four blocks across. Base 2 (right): every prime is in the upper half.
cards.explained: The height is the reversed number, so its first digit is the last digit of n: a prime ends in 1, 3, 7 or 9, hence four bands, and in base 2 in 1, hence the upper half. A reversal can be prime only if it ends in 1, 3, 7 or 9 itself, that is if n starts with one of them: four blocks. n and its reversal have the same digit sum, so the same remainder mod 9, and the same remainder up to sign mod 11: the reversal of a prime is never a multiple of 3 or 11. That makes it (10/4)·(3/2)·(11/10) = 4.13 times as likely to be prime as a number of its size; in base 2 the factor is 2·(3/2) = 3.
cards.checked: Reversible primes with 1 to 6 digits: 4, 9, 43, 204, 1,499, 9,538, predicted 6, 12, 44, 235, 1,463, 9,843. In base 2 that prediction is short (20 bits: 9,210 found, 8,552 predicted), because primes with a short period tie n to its reversal as well: the reversal of a 20-bit prime is a multiple of 7 for only 11.0% of them. See the card 'Found along the way'.
cards.exponents: The exponents. 13 of the 52 have a prime reversal in base 10 (2, 3, 5, 7, 13, 17, 31, 107, 1,279, 9,941, 3,021,377, 13,466,917 and 136,279,841), where 14.1 are expected; 16 in base 2, where 20.4 are expected. Ordinary.

cards.name: Survivors of the sieve up to P
cards.short: Throw out every number with a factor up to P: what is left is coin flips, fair at P = N^0.4
cards.verdict: theorem (Buchstab) for the count; the fair coin is Hardy–Littlewood
cards.seen: Left (P = 7, enlarged): a weave, light and dark in a rhythm. Right (P = 197): light with dark specks at random; nothing to see.
cards.explained: With P = 7 only the numbers with no factor 2, 3, 5 or 7 are left, 48 of every 210. In a width of 48 a column is one remainder mod 210, and the multiples of 11 are every 11th dot of it, those of 13 every 13th: the weave is the next primes of the sieve. With P near N^0.4 the sieve has done all it can, and whether a survivor is prime behaves like the flip of a coin.
cards.checked: P = 7: 114,286 survivors up to 500,000, 41,534 of them prime; every column one remainder mod 210 and the multiples of 11, 13 and 17 exactly every 11th, 13th and 17th dot (0 exceptions); two primes in a row 14,596 times, 0.957 of the coin's share. P = 197 = N^0.403: 51,082 survivors, 41,493 prime; two in a row 34,020 times, 1.000 of the coin's share. The count against Mertens' product: 0.998 (P = 7) and 1.019 (P = 197); for large numbers that ratio is Buchstab's 1/(e^γ·ω(u)), which is 1 at P = N^0.4027.

cards.name: Scales: left half against right half
cards.short: The rows narrow on a straight line in ln H; the long rows are the zeta zeros
cards.seen: Fifteen rows. The top rows are a few sharp lines, the middle rows clouds, the bottom rows single wavy curves, and the rows get narrower downwards (right: the lower left, three times enlarged).
cards.explained: Row k compares the primes in the H = 2<sup>k</sup> numbers left of n with those in the H numbers right of n, in units of what coin flips would give. With H = 1 the difference is −1, 0 or 1: three lines. Coin flips would make every row equally wide. The primes are spread more evenly than that, the more so the longer the window. In the bottom rows neighbouring windows overlap almost wholly, so the dots join into a curve, and the curve is made of zeta zeros: a window of half-width H at n hears the zeros near the height π·n/H.
cards.checked: Mean square by row up to 500,000: 0.93 (H = 1), 0.76 (8), 0.59 (64), 0.42 (512), 0.28 (4,096), 0.18 (16,384); coins give 0.92 in every row. Slope 0.055 per doubling of H against ln 2/ln n = 0.057; up to a million 0.055 against 0.054, up to 100,000 0.067 against 0.066. Rebuilt from the first 160 zeta zeros, without a single prime, the bottom rows correlate 0.940 (H = 16,384), 0.904 (8,192) and 0.841 (4,096) with the picture. A decoy fails here and only here: numbers with no factor up to 47 that pass a coin, drawn on 10 to 30 million, keep 0.58 of the coin's variance from H = 2,048 on, while the primes fall from 0.46 to 0.21 at H = 131,072.

cards.name: Atlas of the polynomials m² + m + A
cards.short: Every line of the square layouts as a column, sorted: the order is the class number
cards.seen: A field fading from light on the left to dark on the right, with dark horizontal rows on the right (right picture: the top-left corner, five times enlarged).
cards.explained: A column is one polynomial m² + m + A, its values downwards, the columns sorted by their number of primes. Bateman and Horn: the count is C(A)·Σ 1/ln(value), where C(A) multiplies, over the primes p, by how often p fails to divide the values; that depends only on whether D = 1 − 4A is a square mod p. The class number formula turns the same product into, nearly, √|D|/(π·h(D)): few classes for the size of D means few small primes that divide. The dark rows on the right are 3: it divides one value in three when A ≡ 1 (mod 3) and two in three when 3 divides A.
cards.checked: Recounted with a second class-number routine: A = 41 has 270 primes in its first 400 values (the first 40 all prime, the only such column), then 1,997 (219, h = 8), 1,481 (216, h = 7), 107 (213, h = 2); the poorest is 1,743 = 3·7·83 with 16. ln(primes) against ln(√|D|/h): correlation 0.982 over 1,249 columns. Bateman–Horn predicts 99,892 primes in all and 99,345 are there; column by column the correlation is 0.997. The counts differ from the prediction by 0.39 standard deviations of a random count, not 1: random counts around the prediction would correlate 0.961 with √|D|/h, not 0.982. The columns with h = 1 are A = 3, 5, 7, 11, 17 and 41.

cards.name: Spectrum: the zeros in the primes
cards.short: The walk of the primes as waves in ln x: a peak on every zero, of height 1/|ρ|
cards.seen: Sharp peaks on a flat floor, lower and lower to the right, a light line through each (left: zeta; middle: the lanes mod 12; right: mod 19, a million numbers).
cards.explained: By Riemann's formula the walk ψ(x) − x, divided by √x, is a sum of waves cos(γ·ln x), one for each zero ½ + iγ, of strength 2/|ρ|. The picture measures the strength of every wave from the primes on the page alone; the light lines are the known zeros. With a character (P = 4, 8, 12 or a prime) the walk is the prime race of that character and the peaks are the zeros of its L-function.
